<div class="pub-group"><div class="year">Thesis</div><ol class="papers">
<li class="paper" data-type="thesis"><div class="paper-title">Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches to Exploring Brain Structural Changes in Alzheimer&rsquo;s Disease Progression: A Longitudinal Study</div><div class="paper-authors"><span class="me">Aboagye, F.</span> (lead author), Dzobo, M. M., &amp; Sackey, R.</div><div class="paper-venue"><span class="chip published">Thesis</span>Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of Ghana, November 2025 <a class="plink" href="files/Alzheimers_Research.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PDF</a></div>
<details class="abs"><summary>Abstract</summary><p>Alzheimer&rsquo;s disease is a leading cause of cognitive decline in older adults, and timely intervention depends on recognising dementia progression early. This project examines how changes in brain structure and cognition track dementia severity over time, using the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS) longitudinal MRI dataset: 150 adults aged 60 to 96, scanned across 373 sessions at least a year apart.</p><p>A repeated-measures MANOVA showed that demented, non-demented and converted participants differ on cognition and brain structure combined (Pillai&rsquo;s trace = 0.446, <em>p</em> &lt; 0.001), with large effects for MMSE score and normalised whole-brain volume. Principal component analysis condensed eight clinical and imaging measures into five components that retain 91.7% of the variance, and K-means clustering on these components revealed five distinct subgroups. After correcting class imbalance with SMOTE, five classifiers were built in R and evaluated with cross-validation and held-out test data. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting were the most accurate (93.1% and 92.6%), while a neural network best distinguished between severity levels (AUC = 0.919). Age, MMSE, normalised whole-brain volume and estimated intracranial volume emerged as the strongest predictors. The results show that combining statistical inference with machine learning gives an accurate and interpretable framework for tracking dementia severity. They also point to routine MRI and cognitive measures as practical markers for earlier detection.</p></details></li>
</ol></div>

<li class="paper" data-type="project"><div class="paper-title">Exploring the Design and Implementation of Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS)</div><div class="paper-authors"><span class="me">Aboagye, F.</span></div><div class="paper-venue"><span class="chip progress">Project</span>Department of Economics, University of Ghana, October 2024</div>
<details class="abs"><summary>Summary</summary><p>This research examined the design and implementation of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), with emphasis on survey design, sampling methodology, questionnaire development, field implementation, and data quality assurance. It explored how nationally representative household surveys generate reliable statistics on health, education, child protection, nutrition, and other Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicators, highlighting the role of official statistics in evidence-based policymaking and national development planning.</p></details></li>
